drafts.title: Reduce perceived harshness on broken pavement so rides feel comfortable on rough roads
drafts.description: Customers experience a noticeably smoother ride over broken pavement and municipal repair seams: occupants should not describe the ride as 'harsh' during typical urban and suburban routes with poor surface quality.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On a standardized 5 km rough-road validation route driven at an average speed of 45 mph, at least 80% of a blinded test group (n≥30) must rate the ride as 'comfortable' or better; objective body-acceleration metrics on the route must show a reduction in RMS vertical acceleration by ≥20% compared to the current model.
assumptions: Validation route and test protocol are defined and repeatable (same road segment, vehicle load, tire specification).
Adaptive dampers or comparable chassis control available in successor variants to tune ride response.
Comparisons are against the current-generation baseline measured with the same test protocol.
uncertainties: Local road quality varies; improvements on extremely broken roads may be limited by tire and geometry trade-offs.
Perceived comfort is partly subjective; we mitigate with both user ratings and objective acceleration metrics.

drafts.title: Limit distracting wind noise at highway speeds above 70 mph
drafts.description: Customers do not perceive wind noise as distracting when cruising on highways above 70 mph; cabin wind noise remains low and non-fatiguing for driver and passengers.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a steady-state highway test at 75 mph (120 km/h) with windows closed and outside crosswinds ≤10 mph, interior A-weighted sound level at the driver ear must be ≤68 dB(A); in addition, fewer than 10% of test participants (n≥30) report wind-related distraction in a blinded evaluation.
assumptions: Tests run on representative highway sections with consistent wind/weather conditions.
Measurement point standardized at driver-ear location and vehicle load representative of two occupants.
uncertainties: Exterior mirrors, roof racks, or optional accessories can affect wind noise; accessory configurations must be controlled during testing.
Extreme crosswinds or aftermarket changes may degrade performance beyond the target.

drafts.title: Make lane-keeping assist steer smoothly through curves, eliminating abrupt interventions
drafts.description: When lane-keeping assist is engaged on curves, customers experience smooth, predictable steering corrections without abrupt or jerky inputs.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In 100 validated curve maneuvers across a range of radii and speeds (40–70 mph), fewer than 5 interventions are classified by test drivers as 'abrupt' (driver-reported) and objective lateral-jerk measurements exceed the abruptness threshold in fewer than 5% of maneuvers.
assumptions: Test maneuvers and driver rating scale are defined in advance and use the current-generation baseline for comparison.
Lane-keeping assist remains an opt-in driver aid and operates within system limits; performance evaluated on well-marked highways.
uncertainties: Very poor lane markings, heavy crosswinds, or sensor obstructions may still require driver takeover and can trigger stronger interventions.
What a driver perceives as 'abrupt' varies; we combine subjective ratings with objective jerk metrics to reduce ambiguity.

drafts.title: Offer at least one powertrain variant that delivers 600 miles real-world range between refuels/charges
drafts.description: Customers can choose a 5 Series configuration that provides a real-world driving range of at least 600 miles on a single tank or single full charge, so long trips require fewer stops.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: At least one available powertrain variant achieves ≥600 miles (≈965 km) real-world range on a representative mixed driving route (combined highway and secondary roads, average speed ~55 mph) as validated by an independent real-world range test protocol.
assumptions: The 600-mile target can be met by an ICE or hybrid variant (not necessarily by every electrified variant).
Real-world validation uses a standardized protocol agreed with certification/validation teams (ambient temperature, load, route).
uncertainties: Pure battery-electric variants achieving 600 miles may not be realistic for all customers within the successor window without breakthroughs in energy density or vehicle mass reduction.
Actual customer range will vary with driving style, speed, ambient temperature and accessory use (HVAC).

drafts.title: Help customers find compatible fast chargers quickly and reliably on trips
drafts.description: When planning or en route, customers see only chargers that are compatible with their vehicle (connector, supported power, payment) and can locate a usable fast charger quickly without confusion.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: During a 200-mile navigation-guided trip test, the route planner must list compatible chargers for the vehicle and, in a user study (n≥30), at least 95% of participants locate a compatible fast charger using the vehicle interface within 5 minutes.
assumptions: Access to up-to-date third-party charging-station data (connector types, real-time availability, payment options) is available via partners or network agreements.
Test participants use typical account/payment setups representative of target customers.
uncertainties: Third-party network outages, incorrect station metadata, or temporary hardware outages at stations can still prevent successful charging despite correct compatibility indicators.
Coverage and data quality vary by geography; performance may be lower in areas with sparse infrastructure.

drafts.title: Make the charge-port indicator show charging state clearly at a glance
drafts.description: Customers understand whether charging is pending, ongoing, completed or faulted from the exterior charge-port indicator without needing to open an app or the trunk.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In daylight at 3 meters distance, in a user test (n≥30) participants correctly identify the charging state (not charging, charging, completed, fault) from the port light in ≥95% of single-glance attempts.
assumptions: Indicator design (color/animation) follows a simple, standardized mapping that users can learn quickly.
Tests conducted in representative daylight conditions and with common ambient lighting variability.
uncertainties: Extreme sunlight angles or occlusions (covers, dirt) may reduce visibility; customer education or secondary indicators (app) can mitigate.
Different color perception among users (color blindness) should be considered in design; tests include varied participants.

drafts.title: Request for Level 3 automated driving approval in Germany (regulatory ask — out of scope for product-level requirement)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the car receives type approval for Level 3 automated driving in Germany.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for Type approval for Level 3 automated driving in Germany (as stated in SCOPE-R01).
assumptions: Type approval and homologation are governed by external regulatory bodies and legal frameworks.
uncertainties: Approval timelines, required certifications and legal responsibilities are outside product design control.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory/homologation request — must be handled via compliance/homologation tracks rather than a customer-facing vehicle requirement.

drafts.title: Request that the powertrain complies with CARB emission limits in all US states (regulatory ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers request the powertrain complies with CARB emission limits so the vehicle can be sold and used across all US states.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for CARB-compliant powertrain availability in all US states (as stated in SCOPE-R03).
assumptions: Regulatory certification and state-level approvals are managed by compliance teams.
uncertainties: Implementation and timing depend on certification processes and legal frameworks.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory/homologation request — outside direct product-experience requirement scope.

drafts.title: Request for UN R155 cybersecurity type approval (regulatory ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers expect the vehicle to fulfil UN R155 cybersecurity type approval.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for UN R155 cybersecurity type approval (as stated in SCOPE-R06).
assumptions: Cybersecurity certification requires specific organizational processes and evidence submission to authorities.
uncertainties: Certification scope and timelines depend on evolving regulation and authority interpretation.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory/certification request — handled by compliance and security engineering rather than as a customer-facing requirement.

drafts.title: Request that the battery complies with the EU battery passport regulation (regulatory ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the battery complies with EU battery passport requirements.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for battery passport compliance (as stated in SCOPE-R07).
assumptions: Battery passport implementation and reporting are compliance deliverables managed by regulatory/product compliance teams.
uncertainties: Scope and data requirements of the battery passport may evolve with regulation and regional differences.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory/compliance request — out of direct customer-outcome scope.

drafts.title: Request for 800 V electrical architecture (engineering-spec ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the car uses an 800 V electrical architecture.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for an 800 V electrical architecture (as stated in SCOPE-E01).
assumptions: Electrical architecture choices are an engineering design decision with implications for suppliers, charging compatibility and cost.
uncertainties: Adoption feasibility depends on supplier availability, packaging, and cost trade-offs for the successor vehicle.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification request — requires technical evaluation rather than a direct customer-facing requirement.

drafts.title: Request to upgrade onboard AC charger to 22 kW (engineering-spec ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the onboard AC charger be upgraded to 22 kW.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for a 22 kW onboard AC charger (as stated in SCOPE-E03).
assumptions: Onboard charger power is an engineering/spec decision with impacts on thermal, packaging and cost.
uncertainties: Real-world benefit depends on availability of 3-phase 22 kW AC charging infrastructure in target markets.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification request — not a customer-facing outcome by itself.

drafts.title: Request for solid-state cells with 400 Wh/kg (engineering-spec ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the battery uses solid-state cells with 400 Wh/kg energy density.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for solid-state cells at ~400 Wh/kg energy density (as stated in SCOPE-E06).
assumptions: Solid-state cell availability, maturity and supplier readiness determine feasibility.
Energy-density targets depend on future cell technology roadmaps and supply agreements.
uncertainties: Commercial availability and safety validation timelines for such cells are uncertain within a 3–5 year horizon.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification request — technology candidate that requires R&D and supplier commitments.

drafts.title: Request for 395 mm front brake discs (engineering-spec ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the front brake discs have a diameter of 395 mm.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: desire for 395 mm front brake disc diameter (as stated in SCOPE-E07).
assumptions: Brake component dimensions are an engineering choice affecting caliper design, wheel fitment and unsprung mass.
uncertainties: Fitment and trade-offs with wheel sizes, weight and thermal performance must be evaluated by engineering.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification request — not a direct customer-facing requirement.

drafts.title: Request that highway assist uses a lidar sensor from a named supplier (engineering-spec ask — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers ask that highway assist uses a lidar sensor from a named supplier.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Customer signal: preference that highway assist uses a lidar sensor from a named supplier (as stated in SCOPE-E08).
assumptions: Choosing specific suppliers is a procurement and engineering decision driven by performance, cost and availability.
uncertainties: Supplier availability, qualification timelines and integration complexity may prevent use of a specific supplier at launch.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering supplier-spec request — procurement/engineering decision rather than a customer-facing acceptance criterion.
